claim: Even a mainstream, actively developed (2026) experimentation product does not yet let a caller pin an experiment to a specific dataset version -- it always runs against the latest -- which is a concrete gap in variant addressing/versioning practice, stated directly by the vendor rather than inferred.
query: Langfuse experiments documentation prompt variant dataset
read: If a dataset is hosted on Langfuse, "the SDK will automatically create a dataset run for you that you can inspect and compare in the Langfuse UI"; for a local dataset only traces and evaluation scores are tracked, with no dataset run object at all. On versioning specifically the docs concede a present limitation: "Experiments always run on the latest dataset version at experiment time. Support for running experiments on specific dataset versions will be added to the SDK shortly." Isolation from production is structural rather than an explicit mechanism: experiment traces are tagged as part of a dataset run, distinguishing them from production traffic within the same project workspace, but the docs do not describe a dedicated isolation boundary.

claim: Isolation for an agent (as opposed to a stateless prompt call) is discussed at the execution-sandbox level -- filesystem/network/host containment of the running process -- which is a distinct axis from traffic-routing isolation (shadow/canary/A-B); a full isolated-experiment design for agents needs both axes.
query: offline replay recorded agent runs sandbox evaluation trajectory 2026
read: An agent execution sandbox is defined as "a production isolation boundary for AI-generated code because it restricts filesystem access, network egress, and host interaction independently of the agent's decisions." Three isolation tiers are distinguished: standard Docker containers ("the workload is only one system call away from host compromise"), gVisor user-space syscall interception (an escape requires exploiting "two independent codebases"), and Firecracker microVMs (hardware-level isolation, boot under 125ms, ~5 MiB memory overhead per microVM, but limited GPU support). Layered controls beyond the isolation tier itself: read-only root filesystems, default-deny network egress, cgroup resource limits, immutable configuration files.
snippet: with standard containers, the workload is only one system call away from host compromise
title: What Is an Agent Execution Sandbox? | Augment Code
topic: Sandbox isolation mechanisms (containers, gVisor, Firecracker microVMs) available for isolating an agent variant's execution

claim: This is the clearest, most specific found answer to 'what does isolation mean here': a three-stage progression (shadow -> canary -> ramp) plus deterministic cohort-stable hashing so a given user/tenant always lands in the same arm, plus an automatic eval-gated rollback -- not a single mechanism but a pipeline of them.
query: agent platform prompt experimentation A/B testing shadow traffic 2026
read: The staged rollout sequence is stated plainly: "Shadow first, canary second, ramp third." Shadow runs both variants against live inputs without serving the new prompt's output, validating offline predictions before any user sees it. Canary then serves the new variant to "1-5 percent of cohort traffic" using "cohort-stable hashing (hash user-id or tenant-id modulo bucket count) so a user stays in the same arm." For statistical rigor, matched-pair design ("same inputs, both prompts") is used because it gives "one to two orders of magnitude tighter CI" than independent-group testing; sample sizing follows n_per_arm = 16 * sigma_squared / MDE_squared, and teams "ship only when the CI sits entirely on one side of zero," using "10,000 resamples of paired deltas." Post-ship, a "15-minute rolling per-rubric pass rate" auto-reverts a variant if a rubric drops below 1.5x its noise floor.
snippet: Shadow first, canary second, ramp third.
title: A/B Testing LLM Prompts: The Statistical Playbook (2026)
topic: Current staged-isolation practice for LLM/agent A-B tests: shadow first, canary second, ramp third; cohort-stable hashing; matched-pair design

claim: No open standard for an experiment definition (over prompts, tools or workflows) was found. The closest published, vendor-neutral schema in this space -- OpenTelemetry's GenAI semantic conventions -- is itself still pre-1.0/Development as of mid-2026 and explicitly does not cover experiment/variant/A-B-test attributes; anyone wanting this today is told to invent a private namespace. This absence is itself the finding, not a search failure.
query: OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions evaluation experiment span attributes 2026
read: Confirmed directly: "as of July 17, 2026, no GenAI-specific span, event, metric, or attribute in the dedicated repository is marked Stable; the GenAI conventions remain Development." More importantly for this question, the piece covers existing span types (invoke_agent, chat, execute_tool), message structures, token usage and evaluation events, but describes no dedicated semantic conventions for A/B testing, prompt variants, or experimental workflows at all -- the only experiment-adjacent knob is an opt-in flag selecting which generation of the schema to use ("setting OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN=gen_ai_latest_experimental selects the latest experimental conventions"), which controls schema version, not experiment/variant tracking. Guidance for anyone needing it: "Keep custom attributes out of gen_ai.*" -- i.e., build your own namespace.

claim: For agents specifically (as opposed to a single-turn prompt call), current practice frames isolation as 'runs, decides, but does not act' -- the agent's proposed action is compared against the real outcome per-case rather than against an aggregate metric, and promotion out of the shadow is a staged autonomy ladder, not a single traffic-percentage ramp.
query: buildmvpfast "A/B Testing AI Agents" shadow deployment production behavior
read: Core mechanism, stated directly: "In shadow mode, the agent processes the same inputs as the production workflow but does not execute the final action." The existing system (human or current automation) stays the actual decision-maker while the candidate agent runs in parallel, which surfaces "messy real-world inputs, timing issues, missing context, edge-case workflows, human override patterns" that offline eval misses. The operational unit of isolation-testing is disagreement, not aggregate score: "Capture disagreements as the main event" between agent and baseline, requiring "observability, not vibes" -- tracking inputs, retrieved context, proposed actions, confidence signals and reviewer verdicts per case. Graduation out of shadow mode is staged: "promote in steps: Suggest only -> Human approves with one click -> Agent executes low-risk cases automatically -> Expand scope gradually."
snippet: In shadow mode, the agent processes the same inputs as the production workflow but does not execute the final action.
title: Shadow Mode for AI Agents: Test Real Workflows Before You Grant Real Power | AgentForge Hub
topic: Shadow mode specifically for autonomous agents (not stateless prompt calls): parallel execution without taking the final action, disagreement logging as the primary signal

claim: Of the four named strategies, only shadow testing gives true production isolation (candidate output never reaches a user); A/B and canary both let real users experience the candidate (differing only in random vs. deterministic assignment and exposure ramp), and interleaved testing exposes the candidate inside a live response. 'Isolation' is therefore not one technique but a spectrum, and shadow is the end of that spectrum closest to what a self-improvement loop's 'trial in isolation before touching production' stage needs.
query: buildmvpfast "A/B Testing AI Agents" shadow deployment production behavior
read: Four distinct isolation strategies, each with a load-bearing distinction: A/B testing splits traffic non-uniformly ("incoming traffic is split between two versions of a system: the existing legacy model (control) and the candidate model (variation)"), typically 90/10, with real users seeing whichever arm they're assigned. Canary "targets a specific subset and progressively increases exposure if performance metrics indicate success," using deterministic (not random) user assignment so the same users stay on the candidate across phases. Interleaved testing "combines predictions from both models in real time" within a single response (e.g. "some items in the recommendation list may come from the legacy model, while others are generated by the candidate model"). Shadow testing is the fully isolated case: "the candidate model runs in parallel with the legacy model and receives the same live requests as the production system. However, only the legacy model's predictions are returned to users, while the candidate model's outputs are simply logged."
snippet: the candidate model runs in parallel with the legacy model and receives the same live requests as the production system. However, only the legacy model's predictions are returned to users, while the candidate model's outputs are simply logged.
title: Safely Deploying ML Models to Production: Four Controlled Strategies (A/B, Canary, Interleaved, Shadow Testing) - MarkTechPost
